sections.title: The Parable of the Lost Sheep
observations: In this parable, Jesus illustrates God's love for the lost by comparing Himself to a shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine sheep to find the one that is lost. This emphasizes the value of each individual to God and His relentless pursuit of those who stray away.
The joy in heaven over one sinner who repents is a central theme, highlighting the importance of repentance and the celebration that follows.
This parable sets the tone for the following stories, reinforcing the idea that God seeks out the lost and rejoices in their return.

sections.title: The Parable of the Lost Coin
observations: Similar to the previous parable, this story emphasizes the joy of finding something that was lost. The woman who loses a coin represents God's diligent search for the lost.
The act of sweeping the house and searching carefully illustrates the lengths to which God goes to bring sinners back to Himself.
The communal joy expressed when the coin is found mirrors the joy in heaven, reinforcing the theme of repentance and restoration.

sections.title: The Parable of the Prodigal Son
observations: This is perhaps the most famous of the parables, depicting the journey of a wayward son who squanders his inheritance. It illustrates the themes of sin, repentance, and forgiveness.
The father's response to the son's return is a powerful image of God's grace. Instead of condemnation, the father welcomes the son with open arms, symbolizing God's readiness to forgive.
The older brother's reaction serves as a warning against self-righteousness and jealousy, reminding us that God's grace is available to all, regardless of their past.

importantVerses.commentary: There will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.
Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.
For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to celebrate.

questions: What do these parables reveal about the nature of God and His relationship with sinners?
How do the themes of repentance and forgiveness manifest in our own lives?
In what ways can we be like the older brother, and how can we guard against that attitude?
